FOR INDEPENDENT MEDICAL COURIERS

Price the route, not just the miles.

See whether a clinic, lab, pharmacy, or STAT route covers its paid wait, loaded labor, vehicle cost, temperature-control supplies, and overhead. After using this, you can now see contribution margin per vehicle-hour, which used to take a spreadsheet that hid waiting time.

Route offer

Loaded labor should include payroll burden and non-driving paid time. Consumables can include coolers, labels, gel packs, and spill-kit allocation. Deadhead is the unpaid run to the first stop and back from the last; leave it at zero if the route starts and ends at your door. These are your inputs, not industry standards.

Common questions

What counts as billable wait time on a medical courier route?

Only the minutes beyond the grace period built into your contract. Enter total wait time and the grace period separately — the calculator subtracts one from the other and pays the difference at your loaded labor rate, the same as any other hour on the route.

Why is overhead calculated as a percentage of revenue instead of cost?

Overhead here is a share of the route's revenue, not a markup on your direct costs — enter the percentage of admin, insurance, and facility cost this one route should absorb. That way a large, high-revenue route carries a proportionally larger share of fixed cost than a small one, which a flat per-route overhead figure would not.

What is the difference between contribution margin and margin per vehicle-hour?

Contribution margin is the dollar amount left after labor, vehicle cost, consumables, and overhead are subtracted from revenue. Margin per vehicle-hour divides that figure by the hours the route actually occupies, including billable wait, so you can compare two routes with different time commitments rather than only their total dollars.

Should deadhead miles go in "total miles" or their own field?

Their own field. Total miles is the driving the route pays for; deadhead is the unpaid run from home to the first stop and back from the last, and it burns the same fuel and occupies the same hours. Keeping them apart matters in a negotiation — billable miles are a rate conversation, deadhead is a routing one, and a route whose deadhead is the problem is fixed by a different stop order or a closer starting point rather than by a higher price. On the worked example, 40 deadhead miles and 70 minutes turn a $151.80 margin into $90.33: 40% of the margin, invisible until it has a line of its own.

What should I quote for this route?

The "break-even / stop" and "at target margin / stop" figures. Because overhead here is a percentage of revenue, raising the price also raises the overhead that price has to carry, so break-even is a fixed point rather than a sum of costs. On the worked example the route costs $118.20 in labor, vehicle, and consumables but needs $131.33 to break even — $21.89 a stop — and $28.14 a stop to clear a 20% margin. Those are the numbers to counter with; the offer on the table is what you compare them against.

How far can fuel and maintenance rise before this route stops working?

That is the "break-even $/mile" line: the vehicle cost per mile at which contribution margin reaches zero, holding the price and everything else fixed. On the worked example the route survives up to $5.06 a mile against the $0.72 entered, so fuel is not what threatens it. It reads $0.00 when the route loses money even if driving were free — that is a pricing problem rather than a fuel one, and the break-even per stop is the line to read instead.

Does selecting Scheduled, STAT, or Dedicated change the calculation?

No — route type only labels the copied summary text; every dollar figure comes from the revenue, stops, miles, time, and rate fields you enter. If a STAT route pays more for the same stops and miles, enter its higher revenue and time commitment directly rather than relying on the dropdown to adjust anything.

What does "Copy share link" send, and does anything leave my browser?

It copies the current page's address with every route field, including route type, encoded after a # in the URL. A browser never sends the part after # to a server, so pasting that link into a text or email is the only way the figures travel — opening it re-runs the same route immediately, so a dispatcher or accountant sees the exact offer you priced rather than just the margin you tell them.

is-this-medical-courier-route-worth-it.h.text:
← Medical courier route margin calculator

Is this medical courier route worth it?

A route offer's flat dollar figure does not say whether it covers your real time and vehicle cost. Two routes paying the same amount can have very different margins once paid wait, mileage, consumables, and overhead are counted against them.

Open the free route margin calculator

What a flat route rate hides

Wait time beyond the grace period. Clinics, labs, and pharmacies rarely have a specimen or delivery ready the instant a courier arrives. A contract's grace period absorbs some of that; everything past it is calendar time the courier is not free to use elsewhere.

Loaded labor, not a driver's take-home rate. Payroll burden and non-driving paid time belong in the labor figure, or the margin looks better than the route actually pays.

Per-mile vehicle cost and per-stop consumables. Fuel, maintenance, and depreciation scale with miles; coolers, labels, and gel packs scale with stops. Both are real costs a flat per-route rate can obscure.

Worked example

A scheduled route paying $300 for 6 stops over 35 miles, 2.5 scheduled hours, 45 minutes of wait against a 15-minute grace period, a $28/hour loaded labor rate, $0.72/mile vehicle cost, $1.50 per-stop consumables, and 10% overhead:

FigureValue
Billable wait30 minutes (45 minus the 15-minute grace)
Labor cost$84.00 (3.0 paid hours at $28)
Vehicle cost$25.20 (35 miles at $0.72)
Consumables$9.00 (6 stops at $1.50)
Overhead (10% of revenue)$30.00
Direct cost$148.20
Contribution margin$151.80 (50.6% of revenue)
Margin per vehicle-hour$50.60

This is contribution margin before taxes and owner draw, not take-home profit — a positive result is a starting point for deciding whether the contract is worthwhile, not a guarantee that it is.

Common questions

How do I know if a medical courier route is profitable?

Subtract loaded labor (including paid wait beyond any grace period), vehicle cost per mile, per-stop consumables, and overhead from the route's revenue to get contribution margin. A $300 route with 6 stops, 35 miles, 2.5 scheduled hours, and 45 minutes of wait with a 15-minute grace period costs $148.20 in direct costs, leaving a $151.80 margin — 50.6% of revenue, before taxes and owner draw.

Should wait time at a clinic or lab count as billable?

Only the wait beyond whatever grace period is built into the contract. With a 15-minute grace period against 45 minutes of actual wait, 30 minutes counts as billable time and is paid at the loaded labor rate like any other hour on the route — the first 15 minutes is absorbed as normal route friction.

What is contribution margin per vehicle-hour and why does it matter more than total margin?

Total margin does not say whether a route is a good use of a limited number of driving hours in a day. Margin per vehicle-hour divides the contribution margin by the hours the route actually occupies — including billable wait — so two routes with the same dollar margin but different time commitments can be compared directly.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Medical Courier Route Margin Calculator

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet

A route-pricing spreadsheet can total labor, vehicle cost, and consumables correctly if every cell is filled in. What it usually has no column for is the unpaid drive to the first stop and back from the last, and when it quotes a new route it usually adds a target margin on top of cost instead of solving for the price that still clears that margin once overhead — a share of the price itself — comes out of it. Both mistakes are quiet: the sheet still balances, it is just wrong.

What a per-route spreadsheet tracks, and what it doesn't

A per-route pricing spreadsheetThis calculator
Labor, vehicle cost, consumablesCells most couriers already trackItemized fields for each, same math
Deadhead (drive to first stop, home from last)No natural column -- the sheet is built from miles and time between stopsSeparate required fields, folded into both cost and paid hours
Wait time past a contracted grace periodTracked once someone thinks to subtract the grace periodSubtracted automatically before it is billed at the labor rate
Quoting a new route to hit a target marginUsually a flat percentage added on top of costSolves for the price where overhead, charged as a percentage of that same price, still leaves the target margin

One route, two margins, twelve miles apart

Take the calculator's own default route: $300 for 6 stops over 35 miles, 2.5 scheduled hours, 45 minutes of wait against a 15-minute grace period, a $28/hour loaded labor rate, $0.72/mile vehicle cost, $1.50 per-stop consumables, and 10% overhead. With no deadhead entered, that route holds up well:

FigureNo deadhead columnWith a real 12 mi / 25 min deadhead leg
Direct cost$148.20$168.51
Contribution margin$151.80$131.49
Margin rate50.60%43.83%

The route did not change. It always had a 12-mile drive to the first stop and back from the last, costing $20.31 in fuel, maintenance, and paid time that a spreadsheet built from stop-to-stop miles and scheduled hours has nowhere to put. Leave that column out and the same route reads as six points of margin better than it is.

Quoting a new route: solving for margin isn't the same as solving for margin and overhead

Say a courier is pricing a brand-new route with the same no-deadhead costs above -- $84 labor, $25.20 vehicle, $9 consumables, $118.20 total -- against a 20% target margin and the same 10% overhead. A spreadsheet built to solve "what price clears 20% margin on revenue" divides cost by one minus that margin, and stops there -- overhead never enters the division because it hasn't been added to cost yet:

Naive quote (margin only)$118.20 ÷ (1 − 20%) = $147.75
Margin actually realized at that price, once 10% overhead is billed on it$14.78, or 10.00% — half the 20% target
This calculator's quote (margin and overhead, same pass)$118.20 ÷ (1 − 20% − 10%) = $168.86

The naive quote undercounts because overhead is 10% of whatever the route bills, not 10% of the cost already on the sheet -- so it has to sit in the same division as the margin, not be added afterward. Leave it out of that division and the price still looks correctly marked up while the overhead it was supposed to fund eats half the intended margin. This calculator solves for the price with both terms in the same denominator, so the margin it prints is the margin the route actually clears.

Open the Medical Courier Route Margin Calculator to price your own route, read is this medical courier route worth it? for the break-even and billable-wait walkthrough, or see this calculator vs. Onfleet if you're weighing dispatch software instead.

Common questions

What does a route-pricing spreadsheet usually get right, and what does it miss?

Filled in carefully, a spreadsheet can total labor hours, vehicle cost per mile, and per-stop consumables correctly. What it usually doesn't have is a column for deadhead -- the unpaid drive from home to the first stop and back from the last -- because a route sheet is normally built from the miles and time between stops, and deadhead is neither. Left out, the sheet reports a route as more profitable than it is.

Why does leaving out deadhead change the margin so much?

Deadhead miles cost the same fuel and maintenance as billed miles, and deadhead minutes occupy the same paid hour as time between stops -- they just carry no revenue. A route that looks like a healthy 50.6% margin with no deadhead line can drop to 43.8% once a real 12-mile, 25-minute deadhead leg is counted, because the labor and vehicle cost were always there; the spreadsheet just never asked about them.

Why can't I just add my target margin on top of the cost to get a quote?

Because overhead here is charged as a percentage of the price you quote, not of the cost you already know -- so raising the price to hit a margin also raises the overhead that price has to carry. Adding a flat percentage on top of cost ignores that second effect and quietly funds too little overhead, which understates the price needed and overstates the margin actually realized.

Does this calculator store or upload anything I type?

No. Every field runs in your browser and nothing is uploaded. Do not enter patient, specimen, or protected health information -- none of the fields need it.

vs-onfleet.html.text:
← Medical Courier Route Margin Calculator

This calculator vs. Onfleet

Two different shapes: Onfleet is an account-based dispatch and route-optimization platform for running a delivery fleet's day. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — does this one route, priced from its stops, wait, deadhead, and costs, actually pay before you quote it or accept it.

What each tool is for

Onfleet is a last-mile delivery management platform, founded in 2012 and headquartered in San Francisco. It is built for businesses that dispatch a fleet of drivers, and it specifically markets a medical delivery offering used by pharmacies, clinical labs, and hospitals — automated route optimization across many stops and drivers at once, live driver tracking, delivery-window and ETA notifications, and proof-of-delivery capture such as signatures, barcode scans, and ID verification to keep a chain-of-custody trail on every stop. It is an account-based platform: a business signs up and runs its whole delivery operation through it as an ongoing subscription, not a one-off calculator. Onfleet's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — a dispatch and route-optimization platform marketed to medical courier, pharmacy, and lab delivery operations, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Onfleet appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Onfleet does. It does not dispatch a driver, optimize a multi-stop sequence, track a vehicle live, or capture proof of delivery, and it stores no route or chain-of-custody record on a server. It takes one route's revenue, stop count, miles, scheduled time, wait time against a contracted grace period, deadhead miles and minutes to and from the first and last stop, loaded labor rate, vehicle cost per mile, per-stop consumables, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the contribution margin, the margin per vehicle-hour, the cost per stop, and the per-stop rate the route needs to break even or clear a target margin — the arithmetic a courier needs before deciding whether to run the route at all. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I run a courier fleet and need to dispatch drivers, optimize multi-stop routes live, and prove chain of custody across every delivery.Onfleet, or a comparable dispatch and route-optimization platform — running live fleet operations is not something this calculator does.
Does this route offer actually pay for its own paid wait, deadhead, labor, and vehicle cost?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
What per-stop rate do I need to counter a broker or facility offer with, to break even or clear a target margin?This calculator's break-even and target-margin figures.
How much does clinic or lab wait time beyond the contracted grace period actually cost this route?This calculator's billable-wait line item, not a flat per-route rate.
I need real-time driver tracking, automated route sequencing, and proof-of-delivery capture across my whole fleet.Onfleet — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
How does the math behind a medical courier route's margin actually work?This calculator's own worked margin guide.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. Onfleet is used through a subscription account.

Most medical courier operations get different value from each: Onfleet (or a comparable dispatch platform) for running the fleet's live routing, tracking, and chain-of-custody paperwork as an ongoing subscription, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to whether one route's offer is worth taking, before any dispatch software is involved. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a dispatched route, a tracked delivery, or a chain-of-custody record.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Onfleet?

They do different jobs, and a medical courier operation of any size may end up using both. Onfleet, founded in 2012 and headquartered in San Francisco, is a last-mile delivery platform that pharmacies, clinical labs, and courier fleets use for dispatch, real-time driver tracking, proof of delivery, and automated route optimization across every driver and every day, sold as an ongoing subscription account. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from a route's revenue, stops, miles, scheduled time, wait against a grace period, deadhead, loaded labor rate, vehicle cost per mile, per-stop consumables, overhead, and target margin, it turns that into the contribution margin, the margin per vehicle-hour, and the per-stop rate the route needs to break even or clear a target margin, before any of it touches a dispatch or tracking system. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A courier operation that already needs to dispatch drivers, optimize multi-stop routes live, and prove chain of custody across a fleet is better served by Onfleet or a comparable platform; a courier who wants an instant, private answer to whether one route's offer is worth taking before it is ever dispatched is in the right place here.
